children: The Japanese automaker plans to develop a new class of range-extender electric vehicles (REEVs) that combine a smaller battery with an onboard generator, offering another pathway for EV adoption as manufacturers grapple with battery costs, charging infrastructure gaps and range anxiety.

“Each country has its own generation mix and fuel conditions; the state of infrastructure development is also different, so which power source is optimal varies by region,” Suzuki Motor Corp President Toshihiro Suzuki said while outlining the company’s Technology Strategy 2026 in Japan on Friday.

India is increasingly becoming the proving ground for Suzuki’s multi-powertrain strategy spanning battery EVs, hybrids, CNG and compressed biogas, while also growing in importance as a manufacturing and export hub.
“Technology is shared. Products are regionally optimised,” Suzuki said, explaining how technologies developed in Japan are transferred to Maruti Suzuki and adapted for local markets.
Chief Technology Officer Katsuhiro Kato outlined a series-hybrid system for compact cars in which a fuel-powered generator produces electricity while an electric motor drives the wheels.

Suzuki plans to add external charging capability and a “right-sized” battery to create what it calls REEV Light, one that “does not carry an oversized battery yet lets you drive without worrying about the remaining charge.”

The concept aligns with Suzuki’s “lean-battery” philosophy, which aims to match battery size to real-world usage, reducing weight, cost and resource consumption. The company has not disclosed battery capacity, electric-only range or engine specifications, nor confirmed an India launch timeline.
Suzuki is not alone in exploring the space. Mahindra & Mahindra is developing range-extender solutions based on its EV architecture, according to people familiar with the company’s product plans.

JSW MG Motor India has also publicly committed to the technology. Director Parth Jindal has said the company plans to introduce range-extender EVs, while its ADAPT architecture is designed to support REEVs alongside battery EVs and plug-in hybrids.

Jindal has highlighted taxation as a key challenge, arguing that lower GST could be critical to making REEVs affordable. He has pointed to the technology’s rapid growth in China and its potential to address range anxiety.

“Range extenders could offer a compelling bridge for India because they allow automakers to size the battery around everyday driving rather than the occasional long-distance journey. That can reduce battery cost and weight while addressing two of the biggest barriers to EV adoption, range anxiety and dependence on public charging infrastructure,” said Randheer Singh, CEO of automotive consulting firm Foresee.

“The bigger question will be how India classifies and taxes these vehicles. If range extenders are to sit between hybrids and pure EVs as a distinct technology, their economics will have to work for both manufacturers and consumers,” Singh said.

India’s importance to Suzuki extends beyond technology development. The company has identified the country as a key global production hub and is targeting annual manufacturing capacity of about four million vehicles by FY2030.

With Suzuki developing REEV Light, Mahindra working on range-extender solutions and JSW MG preparing products based on the technology, India”s next EV battleground may be defined less by whether a vehicle has a battery and more by how much battery it actually needs.

title: Suzuki bets on smaller-battery REEVs as India emerges key battleground
